item.title: Scientists develop “tickle robot” to solve touching mystery
item.description:
Scientists develop “tickle robot” to solve touching mystery

September 14, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Researchers in Nijmegen have set up a laboratory to try to answer one of the oldest questions known to science: why are people ticklish?

Aristotle, Erasmus, Galileo and Darwin all tried to put their finger on the purpose of tickling, or gargalesis to use its scientific name, without finding a definitive reason.

Now two researchers at Radboud University in Nijmegen are using robots and sensors to try to shed more light on the phenomenon.

Tickling exists across cultures and throughout history, but with few variations and little difference between men and women, indicating that it has its roots in biology. Tickling has been observed in other primates such as bonobos and chimpanzees.

Ziliang Xiong and Konstantina Kilteni have set up their lab in a windowless basement in the Maria Montessori building, an environment stripped of any other stimuli that could make their test subjects laugh.

The robot uses a metal pin to simulate tickling, with settings that can be adjusted to measure the effect of different types of contact from gentle stroking to prodding. The participants wear a cap equipped with electrodes that measure their brain responses.

Families and partners

The researchers also asked the 448 subjects to fill in surveys about how they experienced tickling, which revealed strong similiarities.

Most tickling is by adults on children, usually within families, or between siblings. Partners and friends also tickle each other, but this is less common.

Most respondents said they reacted to tickling by laughing, squirming or trying to turn away. The vast majority named the same body parts as most susceptible to tickling: the sides, armpits, belly and the soles of the feet.

The researchers noted that while tickling is associated with play and laughter, many people find it unpleasant and it can quickly become overwhelming. The Nazis even used it as a torture method.

There are indications that people diagnosed with autism are more sensitive to tickling and that ticklish people may even live longer.

Other theories suggest a link between tickling and sexual stimulation, given that couples often tickle each other and it tends to be directed at body parts that are rarely exposed.

Thin skinned

Darwin speculated that tickling felt uncomfortable because it involved touching parts of the body that are unused to being touch, while Aristotle believed it worked on places where the skin is thinner.

But the researchers in Nijmegen said none of the theories provided a complete answer to the reasons why people are sensitive to tickling. “You rarely get touched on your back, but the back is pretty resistant to tickling,” Xiong pointed out.

item.title: Notorious fugitive Dutch arms dealer dies in South Africa
item.description:
Notorious fugitive Dutch arms dealer dies in South Africa

September 14, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A timber merchant turned arms dealer, one of the Netherlands’ most infamous international fugitives, has died peacefully in South Africa after evading justice for years.

Guus Kouwenhoven, who facilitated weapons shipments to the Liberian dictator Charles Taylor in the early 2000s, was sentenced in absentia to 19 years for illegal arms smuggling and complicity in war crimes in 2017.

Despite being arrested in Cape Town, he was released on bail and avoided extradition, living a life of luxury, until his death last week.

Taylor, who was himself given a 50-year prison sentence in The Hague for crimes against humanity, waged civil wars in Liberia until 2003 that killed over 150,000 people. Kouwenhoven’s dealings with him were seen as instrumental to the fighting, which was notorious for its brutality and widespread use of child soldiers.

The Liberian press described Kouwenhoven as a reminder of the country’s violent past, referring to “blood timber”, and asked how someone could get away with turning the timber trade into a currency for war.

So far nothing has been said by Dutch justice minister David van Weel, despite the scale and notoriety of the case. Efforts to have him extradited were complicated and delayed even after South Africa revoked his visa, and his exuberant lifestyle reportedly went unhindered.

Given the recent efforts by Van Weel to push for Sierra Leone to extradite fugitive drugs baron Jos Leijdekkers – even by asking the EU to cut off development aid to the country until it hands him over – Kouwenhoven seems to have escaped proportional scrutiny in his final years, a Volkskrant column argued.

item.title: Woman arrested after trying to hire hitman on dark web scam site
item.description:
Woman arrested after trying to hire hitman on dark web scam site

September 14, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A woman has been arrested for allegedly trying to recruit a hitman on the dark web to kill her ex-husband.

Police confirmed that the 45-year-old woman was arrested in Rotterdam at the weekend for being “involved” in organising a contract killing after the case came to light during an investigation by RTL Nieuws.

The website turned out to be a scam that advertised non-existent “contract killing” services and the attack was never carried out, despite the client transferring US$1,400 (€1,200) in bitcoins as a downpayment.

The man, who was given the cover name of Jerom by RTL, told the broadcaster he was “incredibly relieved that the police have identified a suspect”

The client instructed the website “burn him alive and make sure he doesn’t survive.” When told that the attack would cost $9,000, they replied: “OK, how much does it cost to cut off his arms and legs or shoot him?”

Elderly mother

The instructions included Jerom’s home address, a recent photograph and information about the house, including the alarm system and the fact that his elderly mother lived with him.

“The only demand is that he has to die. I don’t care what happens to the mother,” the client wrote.

Police said arranging the killing was still a crime even though the hitman did not exist. They did not confirm if the request had come directly from the businessman’s ex-wife.

In 2021 a man from The Hague was given an eight-year jail sentence for trying to arrange a murder on the same website. A judge said he had acted “coldly and clinically” in instructing the killing and could take no credit for the fact that the victim was still alive.

item.title: Jetten braced for more tough negotiations to pass budget bill
item.description:
Jetten braced for more tough negotiations to pass budget bill

September 14, 2026 Gordon Darroch

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Prinsjesdag, the first day of the Dutch parliamentary year, should be a high point in the finance minister’s calendar, when he or she sets down the next year’s budget plans in a neat pile and unties the ribbons.

This year, however, Eelco Heinen looks more like a man whose papers have been blown around in a gale, forcing him to scramble around to recover them and tie them up with loose bits of string.

Heinen and Rob Jetten’s hopes of doing a deal with opposition parties before Budget Day on September 15 have been dashed, meaning the minority coalition will now have to find the votes as the bills pass through parliament.

Jetten wanted to agree a package of measures with opposition parties on both left and right, to avoid the “yo-yo politics” that hamstrung his predecessor as prime minister, Dick Schoof.

The talks broke down partly because both sides demanded a high price, but also because the coalition parties were split on what concessions to make.

The outcome is a fudge that appeals to nobody’s taste. And as Jetten has said, the budget that will be presented to parliament next Tuesday is “not the end”. Without an advance deal, the minority coalition will have to keep negotiating to find the 10 seats it needs in the lower house and 16 in the senate.

Spending cuts delayed

Heinen’s party, the right-wing liberal VVD, has had to climb down on its insistence that the €6.5 billion of cuts to welfare spending outlined in the coalition agreement were non-negotiable.

The left-wing opposition party Pro, formerly the alliance of GroenLinks-PvdA, had campaigned to abandon the welfare cuts altogether, supported by the trade unions, who called a one-day nationwide transport workers’ strike last week.

The government wanted to reduce the maximum term for unemployment pay from two years to one, phase out the incapacity benefit IVA and reduce the maximum payment for a range of other benefits, including sick pay and maternity leave, by 20%.

But most of the measures have been postponed by a year rather than cancelled, prompting Pro leader Jesse Klaver to comment that the revised budget was “maybe worse than the original plans”. The unions have said the strikes will continue until the cuts are scrapped.

Cost of living

Klaver told a party congress at the weekend that his party was willing to discuss reforming the WIA incapacity benefit rules, but only if the cuts were taken off the table.

“Pro was founded to combat inequality and strengthen the welfare state,” he said. “You can’t ask us to help you take it apart.”

The left-wing opposition had already forced the cabinet to back down on a proposal to cut the pensions bill by raising the retirement age in step with life expectancy, rather than by eight months for every extra year, which would have saved €2.8 billion a year.

On the right, parties such as JA21 have pressed for the cabinet to make further savings on social security to fund tax cuts across the board and offset the rising cost of living. Inflation is running at 3.3%, driven by soaring fuel and energy prices.

The cabinet has agreed to extend the discount on fuel duty into next year to provide relief for motorists who are paying the highest petrol and diesel prices in Europe.

The cabinet has also allocated €1.7 million to offsetting rising living costs, a response to recent figures from the economic planning bureau CPB that projected a 0.3% drop in spending power next year.

Top earners

With the spending cuts watered down, the government found the money by raising an extra €750 million in income tax on high earners, as well as a small increase in the domestic water levy, according to documents leaked to the commercial broadcaster RTL.

Despite the cash injection, the graphics produced by the finance ministry show that most income groups will still experience a drop in spending power and those who benefit will be pensioners and people on the lowest incomes.

The Telegraaf reported last week that the finance ministry expects the average premium for universal healthcare to go up by €120 a year to €2,028.

The plan to increase the health insurance deductible, or excess, by €60 is also being delayed by a year. It will still rise with inflation for the first time in a decade, so patients will pay €395 up front for medical treatment, €10 more than this year.

Extended negotiation

Part of the reason the negotiations ran into difficulty is that Jetten and Heinen effectively ran parallel talks, with the prime minister trying to agree the political terms while Heinen concentrated on balancing the books.

The VVD finance minister reportedly “shocked” his coalition partners when he produced a draft document that was weighted heavily in favour of right-wing parties such as JA21 and the hardline Protestant SGP, but was unpalatable to the more centrist D66 and CDA, who wanted to bring Pro on board.

After a weekend of emergency talks within the coalition, a revised budget was agreed on Monday, August 31 – the last possible deadline for the draft to be sent to the Council of State for analysis, which is a legal requirement.

At first glance, the revised deal looks like a setback for the VVD, which campaigned during last year’s election and the coalition negotiations that followed on a platform of keeping Pro out of cabinet and marginalising its influence.

With the cabinet lacking a majority in parliament, Pro has a pivotal role as the largest opposition party. Its 20 seats in the Tweede Kamer would give the coalition parties a comfortable majority, while in the upper house the cabinet plus Pro are just two seats short.

Jetten is aware, however, that too many concessions to Pro will risk the balance within his coalition. At some point, Jesse Klaver’s party will have to settle on the welfare cuts, which could test his alliance with the trade unions.

BBB blockers

Another potential stumbling block is the farmers’ party BBB, which was frozen out of the talks because it refused to support the cabinet’s measures to cut nitrogen pollution, which all three coalition parties stand resolutely behind.

The BBB could form a blocking minority in the Senate, where they have 11 seats, and have already threatened to cause trouble over the cabinet’s plans to reform the asset tax system.

The right-wing opposition is larger but disjointed, with Geert Wilders’ PVV and Forum voor Democratie refusing to negotiate in the hope that they can force early elections.

The result is that while parliament has an in-built right-wing majority, it is the left who have had the upper hand in the negotiations so far.

As the budget bill goes through parliament, Rob Jetten faces the double-headed challenge of finding the votes he needs from the opposition while holding his battered coalition together.

item.title: Government bodies collaborate to scrap their penalty payments
item.description:
Government bodies collaborate to scrap their penalty payments

September 14, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Government organisations have been working together to get the financial penalties they owe for missing their deadlines scrapped, an investigation by newspaper Trouw has found.

Officials at the immigration service IND, the benefits agency UWV and the tax office’s benefits arm have been in communication about whether they can push for a complete legal change, freeing them from any fines for failure to comply with their duties.

Internal emails and memos obtained via freedom of information requests show an IND adviser writing to a counterpart at the tax office last year saying they’re looking into abolishing penalties altogether and wants to “see whether abolition for the whole of administrative law is possible”.

Since 2009, anyone whose application for a permit, benefit or allowance is not decided within the legal deadline can be entitled to remedial payments.

The relevant agency is first put on notice, and then if it still fails to decide within two weeks, it owes a daily penalty, rising to a maximum of €1,442, and the applicant can go to court, where a judge can impose an even higher one.

The IND is by far the biggest payer. It paid out nearly €100 million in the first half of this year, almost all of it on asylum cases. Some individual claimants received over €100,000. The agencies say they cannot meet their deadlines because of staff shortages and rising caseloads.

Immigration applicants have already lost the right to automatic penalty payments under an earlier law. In March, MPs from the SGP, ChristenUnie, JA21 and VVD voted to scrap court-imposed ones too, for all immigration cases including residence permits.

The Senate is expected to debate it on September 22, broadcaster NOS reported. Social affairs minister Hans Vijlbrief has said he wants the same for the UWV.
Asked about the emails, an IND spokesperson told Trouw the service is in contact with agencies facing “the same problems” and that “experiences are exchanged”.

item.title: PSV take over at top of Eredivisie after AZ drop first points
item.description:
PSV take over at top of Eredivisie after AZ drop first points

September 14, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Champions PSV Eindhoven took over at the top of the Eredivisie with a 4-1 home win against Sparta after AZ Alkmaar dropped points for the first time this season.

Sparta took the lead in the Philips Stadion when Milan Zonneveld took advantage of a howler by PSV goalkeeper Matej Kovár, who rushed out of his goal to clear a long ball but miskicked.

The home side were back in front by half-time thanks to a header by Sven Mijnans and Kodai Sano’s first goal for his new club. Mijnans went on to complete a hat-trick in the second half, scoring with both feet.

Feyenoord recovered from their 5-1 defeat to Barcelona in midweek to rack up seven goals at PEC Zwolle.

Coach Giovanni van Bronckhorst said his team played “maybe the best half of football I have ever seen from a team I coach” as Nacho Ferri scored a hat-trick and Anis Hadj Moussa netted twice.

AZ took a first-half lead at home to Willem II through Jordy Clasie, but failed to convert their dominance into further goals and were made to pay when Devin Haen equalised nine minutes from the end.

Germans lift Ajax

Ajax’s new German acquisitions played a key role in their 5-1 win at Fortuna Sittard as Julian Brandt opened the scoring with a fierce shot, while Thilo Kehrer marked his debut with a goal and an assist.

Wout Weghorst scored his first goal since arriving at Twente as his penalty helped his team to a 2-0 win against ADO Den Haag, who are bottom of the table with one point from six matches.

Cambuur Leeuwarden became the first of the newly promoted clubs to notch up a win this season as they beat troubled NEC 3-0, with a double from French winger Ilyes Hamache.

Go Ahead Eagles and Groningen remain in the top half of the table after sharing the points in Deventer, while Utrecht notched up their first win under Anthony Correia thanks to a stoppage-time goal by Dani de Wit against Excelsior.

item.title: Energy network charges to rise 19% next year, regulator says
item.description:
Energy network charges to rise 19% next year, regulator says

September 14, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch households will pay an average of €141 more next year for electricity and gas networks, a rise of 19%, according to a preliminary forecast from the consumer and markets regulator ACM.

The increase applies to the fixed network charges (netbeheerkosten) that appear on every energy bill and cannot be reduced by switching supplier, and is on top of the price of gas and electricity itself, which has already risen sharply amid the war in the Middle East.

The electricity component of the charge rises annually by €89 and the gas component by €52, or around €12 a month in total. Network charges will make up about 28% of the average household energy bill in 2027.

The rise varies by network operator. Liander, which covers Amsterdam, most of Noord-Holland and Gelderland, is raising its electricity tariffs by 23%. Stedin, which serves Rotterdam, The Hague and Utrecht, and Enexis, which covers the south and east, are both raising theirs by 17%.

€235 billion rebuild
Network operators say they need to invest around €235 billion in the electricity grid over the next 15 years to connect new housing, offshore wind farms and electrified industry, and there are still around 15,000 businesses, homes, schools and other buildings waiting for a connection.

“This is a lot of money, but the alternative is more expensive,” Liander finance director Walter Bien told NU.nl. Operators put the cost of grid congestion to the economy at €10 billion to €40 billion a year.

The jump in 2027 is partly the result of a new five-year regulatory period which allows operators to pass on investment costs more quickly and to recover cost overruns from the previous five years.

Climate minister Stientje van Veldhoven said in a written response that she understood households found the rise worrying, but that fossil fuels had to be phased out. Energy remains affordable for most people “on average”, she said, and an emergency fund for people unable to pay their energy bills will be available again this winter.

The ACM will set the final tariffs for 2027 in December. From 2029 the Netherlands is expected to move to a new tariff system in which heavy users pay more and the time of day electricity is used also counts.

item.title: Some Dutch people are about to be more equal than others
item.description:
Some Dutch people are about to be more equal than others

September 13, 2026 Robin Pascoe

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Earlier this month the SNBN, a foundation which lobbies for better rights for Dutch nationals who live abroad, held its annual campaign day in The Hague. The event included a panel discussion about legislation which would allow Dutch expats to retain their Dutch nationality if they adopted a second one – and which would also clear the way for more foreigners who become Dutch to keep their original passports as well.

The legislation, drawn up by D66 and the former Labour party, PvdA, has been around for almost 10 years but was dusted off again last year. It should have been debated in parliament in June but that was postponed to October. Now the debate has again been delayed – this time to December 7.

Should all the foreign nationals in the Netherlands who pay tax, contribute to society and would like to become Dutch but can’t because of practical considerations be cheering? Is the country really about to align with most of the rest of Europe and allow dual citizenship? Not at all. If the SNBN panel discussion made anything clear, it is that the VVD – part of the current coalition administration – is not in favour of allowing foreigners dual nationality at all.

Security risk

After all, as MP Bente Becker told the panel, they could be foreign agents, using their diaspora to do the work of foreign governments and posing a security risk. “If you come to the Netherlands, you have to really opt for the Netherlands,” she said. “Being a Dutch citizen,” she added, “is something very special.”

Becker made it clear that without change, her party will not support the legislation – which means, once again, it will either go on the back burner, or the part about extending dual nationality rights to foreigners will be cut out. The CDA, she said, thinks the same way.

D66 MP Jan Schoonis was extremely coy when pressed several times about whether he would be prepared to butcher his party’s bill. “We are here to talk about Dutch people abroad and that is what we are going to organise,” he told the audience. “Everything else we will talk about later.” Not exactly a promising answer.

Exceptions to the rule

I was able to get a Dutch passport while keeping my British one in the wake of Brexit because I am married to a Dutchman and have lived here for over 15 years. I am one of the lucky ones, along with the over-65s who have lived here for a long period, and children who were born here and stayed until the age of 18.

In fact, around 50% of the people becoming Dutch do so by using one of these escape clauses – known as the optieregeling. You opt in to become Dutch. The rest, however, have no choice but to go for naturalisatie and give up their original nationality – with all the problems that can entail.

Discrimination

Legal experts argue that it would be discriminatory to allow people who are originally Dutch to have more than one passport but not new Dutch nationals, and the Council of State, the government’s highest legal authority, has also said that treating people differently would conflict with the constitution.

But the debate about dual citizenship in the Netherlands is not about the legal situation. It is about the loyalty of immigrant groups. Research from 2017 by Maastricht University indicates that the Dutch themselves are more tolerant of Dutch emigrants taking on a second nationality than of immigrants to the Netherlands becoming Dutch and retaining their original one.

The situation is unlikely to have improved since then, given the further rise of the far right.

Anti-foreigner feelings

What the VVD are saying is that Dutch people who are born in the Netherlands and have Dutch parents can have two nationalities without any problem if they move abroad, but those people wishing to become Dutch need to be regarded with suspicion – they must have an ulterior, and possibly sinister, motive if they want to keep their original passports as well.

It’s indicative of the current anti-foreigner sentiment running through large chunks of Dutch society. And it’s a sad reflection on the Netherlands and its “very special” passports.

Do you want to become Dutch and are you faced with giving up your original nationality, or have you already done so? Or have you decided against such a step? We’d like to hear your stories for an article. Please have your say on our social media channels or email, in complete confidence, editor@dutchnews.nl

item.title: Thousands join Amsterdam climate march ahead of budget day
item.description:
Thousands join Amsterdam climate march ahead of budget day

September 12, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Tens of thousands of people marched through Amsterdam on Saturday to call on the government to end its reliance on fossil fuels, three days before the cabinet presents its annual budget plan.

Organisers the Klimaatcrisis Coalitie, an alliance of Greenpeace, Milieudefensie, Extinction Rebellion and around 200 other groups, said more than 40,000 people took part.

The 2.5 kilometre route ran from the Dam to Museumplein, with 43 organised blocs including a youth bloc, a tech bloc and one from trade union federation FNV.

ANP reported many placards had the word “klimaatdrammer” – the “climate nag” label prime minister Rob Jetten adopted as a badge of honour after a VVD MP used it against him in 2019.

The coalition wants the government to end fossil fuel subsidies and speed up the switch to wind and solar rather than nuclear. Spokeswoman Merel Fiets said early reports on the leaked budget were “not encouraging” and that current policy would not meet the climate targets.

Organisers said climate minister Stientje van Veldhoven was handed their demands at a press conference before the march but announced no new measures.

item.title: Cabinet to stop employers docking foreign workers’ pay for rent
item.description:
Cabinet to stop employers docking foreign workers’ pay for rent

September 11, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Employers will no longer be allowed to deduct rent from foreign workers’ minimum wage from July 2028, social affairs minister Hans Vijlbrief has told parliament.

Under current rules, employers and agencies can withhold up to 25% of the minimum wage – around €144 a week – to cover accommodation, provided the housing is certified.

The scheme is used mainly for the estimated 600,000 to 900,000 foreign workers in the Netherlands, most of them from Poland, Romania, Hungary and Ukraine, who work in meat processing, distribution centres and greenhouses.

Research by the ministry found employers regularly deduct the full 25% even when the quality of the housing does not justify it, Vijlbrief wrote in a letter to parliament on Thursday.

He said employers are using the deductions as a “business model” and told Nieuwsuur that too many people are being exploited.

Employers will still be able to provide housing, but will have to charge for it separately and at a fair price, the minister said. Ending deductions will also make it easier for inspectors to check whether workers are actually being paid minimum wage, he said.

The decision is the cabinet’s third on the issue in little over a year. Eddy van Hijum, former social affairs minister, proposed phasing out the deductions from January 2026, but his successor Mariëlle Paul of the VVD reversed that decision, arguing that workers would struggle to find housing without employer involvement.

Trade union federation FNV called the move a “perverse profit model at the expense of migrant workers”, and parliament has twice voted for the deductions to go.

Vijlbrief acknowledged that the ban will mean foreign workers will have to find their own accommodation amid the housing crisis. As a result, the ban will come with a rent protection bill, which has yet to reach parliament. Both are scheduled for July 1, 2028.

The measure is part of a wider package to tackle the exploitation of foreign workers, including a ban on temp agency staff in the meat industry, also from mid-2028. A long-delayed licensing system for staffing agencies is set to take effect in 2027.
